---
title: "Preparing data"
---

Before comparing conditions, bring your measurements and experimental design
together. This guide uses the HepG2 DIA demo to attach sample labels, choose
protein-group quantities, and create a `SummarizedExperiment` for the next steps.
All examples run on the demo database when this page is built.

## 1. Open the demo database

Run these examples in a fresh R session, or reopen the database if you closed it
at the end of [Exploring a database](exploring-a-database.html).

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(ProteoVaultR)
library(dplyr)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r open-vault}
data_dir <- Sys.getenv("PROTEOVAULTR_DEMO_DIR", unset = "demo-data")
vault <- open_vault(
    path = file.path(data_dir, "hepg2_ifna-dia.proteovault.duckdb")
)
vault
```

## 2. Add sample metadata

The HepG2 DIA example contains three control samples and three samples treated
with interferon α-2a for 12 hours. Start by checking the names stored in the vault:

```{r sample-names}
tbl_vault(vault, "samples") %>%
    select(sample_name) %>%
    arrange(sample_name) %>%
    collect() %>%
    knitr::kable(col.names = "Sample name")
```

Create one metadata row per sample. Here, `sample_name` matches the database,
`sample_id` supplies a shorter label, and `condition` records the comparison.
The replicate numbers describe independent biological replicates; matching
numbers across conditions do not establish a paired design.

```{r sample-metadata}
sample_info <- tibble::tribble(
    ~sample_name,   ~sample_id, ~condition, ~biological_replicate,
    "Control_R1",  "Ctrl1",    "Control",  1L,
    "Control_R2",  "Ctrl2",    "Control",  2L,
    "Control_R3",  "Ctrl3",    "Control",  3L,
    "IFNa_12h_R1", "IFNa1",    "IFNa",     1L,
    "IFNa_12h_R2", "IFNa2",    "IFNa",     2L,
    "IFNa_12h_R3", "IFNa3",    "IFNa",     3L
) %>%
    mutate(condition = factor(condition, levels = c("Control", "IFNa")))

vault <- set_sample_metadata(vault, sample_info)

sample_metadata(vault) %>%
    knitr::kable(
        col.names = c("Sample name", "Label", "Condition", "Biological replicate")
    )
```

::: {.alert .alert-warning role="note"}
**Match names exactly:** Keep `sample_name` unchanged and unique. Use `sample_id`
for shorter display labels. Assign the result of `set_sample_metadata()` back to
`vault` so later steps use the attached metadata.
:::

Metadata are attached to this R handle. They do not modify the database, so save
your sample table or analysis script if you want to reuse the assignments later.

## 3. Choose the quantities

Use the protein-group matrix from the HepG2 DIA results, as in the exploration
guide. Resolve its source before exporting:

```{r select-source}
method <- "matrix"
source_id <- resolve_quant_source(
    vault,
    level = "protein_group",
    method = method
)
source_id
```

`matrix` selects the quantities imported from the DIA-NN protein-group matrix.
For a different measurement or database, inspect its source and method inventory
first. Choosing a source makes the selection explicit and keeps measurements
from different files separate.

## 4. Create a SummarizedExperiment

A `SummarizedExperiment` keeps three connected pieces together: the quantity
matrix, sample metadata, and feature annotations. Rows represent protein groups
and columns represent samples. This makes it easier to carry the experimental
design along as you explore and analyze the measurements.

```{r create-experiment}
se <- as_summarized_experiment(
    vault,
    level = "protein_group",
    source_id = source_id,
    method = method,
    samples = sample_info$sample_name
)
se
```

The `samples` argument selects and orders columns using the original sample names.
The `sample_id` labels remain available in the sample metadata. Internal database
sample IDs are retained separately as `vault_sample_id`.

The printed summary shows the matrix dimensions and available annotation columns.
The object contains one assay at this stage:

```{r assay-names}
SummarizedExperiment::assayNames(se)
```

::: {.alert .alert-info role="note"}
**Keep the starting quantities:** Exporting does not add normalization, log
transformation, imputation, or another FDR filter. It preserves the quantities
from your selected source, including any processing already applied upstream.
:::

### 4.1. Check sample order and metadata

Read the sample annotations from `colData`:

```{r inspect-sample-data}
SummarizedExperiment::colData(se) %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    select(sample_name, sample_id, condition, biological_replicate) %>%
    knitr::kable(
        col.names = c("Sample name", "Label", "Condition", "Biological replicate"),
        row.names = FALSE
    )
```

Confirm that the assay columns follow the order you requested:

```{r check-sample-order}
identical(colnames(se), sample_info$sample_name)
```

### 4.2. Inspect quantities and feature annotations

Preview the first five protein groups across the six samples:

```{r preview-assay}
quantity <- SummarizedExperiment::assay(se, "quantity")
quantity[seq_len(5), , drop = FALSE] %>%
    knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

The matrix row names are internal protein-group IDs. Use `rowData` to find the
original group labels and supporting annotations:

```{r inspect-features}
SummarizedExperiment::rowData(se) %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    select(group_id, source_group_id, leading_protein_accession) %>%
    head(5) %>%
    knitr::kable(
        col.names = c("Group ID", "Original group", "Leading protein"),
        row.names = FALSE
    )
```

A row represents a protein group, which can contain several proteins. The leading
accession provides a label; it does not turn a shared group quantity into an
independent measurement for each member.

### 4.3. Check missing values

Missing quantities remain `NA`, while explicit zeros remain zero. Count them
separately before deciding how to handle them:

```{r inspect-missingness}
tibble::tibble(
    sample_name = colnames(quantity),
    missing = colSums(is.na(quantity)),
    zero = colSums(quantity == 0, na.rm = TRUE)
) %>%
    knitr::kable(col.names = c("Sample", "Missing quantities", "Zero quantities"))
```

This is a first check of the selected matrix. Review sample quality and the
pattern of missing values before choosing normalization or imputation.

## 5. Keep the prepared data

The quantities and annotations in `se` are now in R memory, so you can close the
vault and continue working with the prepared object:

```{r close-vault}
close_vault(vault)
vault
```

Keep `se` for the next step: [Quality control](qc.html). It contains the sample conditions,
selected quantities, and protein-group annotations needed to begin inspecting
your samples.
